# Exact structural and heavy-fiber reductions

## Convex hull reduction

Let C be compact and convex, let Lambda=Z^n x R^d, and let S=C intersect Lambda be nonempty. Because C is bounded, S is the finite union of its compact convex fibers and hence compact. Put C'=conv(S). In finite-dimensional Euclidean space the convex hull of a compact set is compact (by Caratheodory, it is the image of a compact product with a compact simplex). Convexity of C gives C' subset C, while S subset C'. Therefore

C' intersect Lambda = S.

In particular every integer fiber remains exactly unchanged. C' can have lower ambient dimension even when C was a convex body; this reduction must be followed by the affine-rank reduction below before reapplying a theorem requiring a convex body.

## Affine-rank reduction in the positive-volume case

Assume q=d, equivalently some integer fiber has positive d-volume. Let A be the affine hull of the finite integer support Z_S={z: C_z is nonempty}, and let r=dim(A). Fix z_* in Z_S. The linear subspace V=A-z_* is spanned by integer vectors. The lattice L=V intersect Z^n has rank r and admits an integer basis b_1,...,b_r. Thus z_*+L=A intersect Z^n.

Let B:R^r -> V send the standard basis to these lattice basis vectors, and define F(t,x)=(z_*+Bt,x). This is an affine isomorphism from R^{r+d} onto A x R^d, carrying Z^r x R^d exactly onto (A x R^d) intersect Lambda. The inverse image of C'=conv(S) is a compact convex set. It is full-dimensional in R^{r+d}: one full d-dimensional fiber supplies all d vertical affine directions, and r affinely independent differences of integer support points supply r independent quotient directions. Thus it is a convex body in the reduced space.

F leaves the continuous coordinate x unchanged, so it preserves each fiber's H_d measure and hence the mixed d-volume sum. No ambient determinant factor should be applied to this fiber measure. Each ambient halfspace restricts under F to a halfspace, the whole reduced space, or the empty set. For a halfspace containing the selected point, the empty case cannot occur. Consequently a theorem with constant 2^{-r} gamma_d in the reduced space proves that same constant for S; this is at least 2^{-n} gamma_d.

If r=d=0, S consists of one point and has depth one. This boundary case is handled directly, rather than invoking a theorem whose dimension-zero ambient space is excluded.

## Heavy-fiber lemma

Let S be a finite union of compact convex fibers in Z^n x R^d, not necessarily the intersection of a full-dimensional body. Put q=max_z dim aff(S_z), M=H_q(S)>0, and m_z=H_q(S_z), where m_z=0 when the fiber dimension is less than q. Suppose some fiber satisfies m_z>=M/2^n.

If q>=1, let g_z be the centroid of S_z in its q-dimensional affine hull, and set y=(z,g_z). Then y belongs to S. For any ambient closed halfspace H containing y, its intersection with the affine hull of this fiber is either the whole affine hull or a q-dimensional closed halfspace containing g_z. Ordinary q-dimensional Gruenbaum therefore gives

H_q(S intersect H) >= H_q(S_z intersect H) >= gamma_q m_z >= 2^{-n} gamma_q M >= 2^{-n} gamma_d M.

The last inequality uses q<=d and the fact that gamma_j=(j/(j+1))^j is decreasing for integers j>=1, with gamma_0=1. To verify monotonicity, the real function h(t)=t log(t/(t+1)) has derivative log(1-1/(t+1))+1/(t+1)<0 for t>0, using log(1-u)<-u.

If q=0, every nonempty fiber is a singleton and its mass is one. Any halfspace containing the selected point includes this unit mass, so the same argument gives depth at least m_z/M>=2^{-n}>=2^{-n}gamma_d.

Thus the heavy-fiber reduction needs only: finite nonempty compact convex fibers; the intrinsic q-dimensional measure; the existence of a fiber carrying at least 2^{-n} of total intrinsic mass; and ordinary continuous Gruenbaum in dimension q. It does not require aligned fibers, an affine centroid map, full-dimensional fibers, lattice width, rationality, a product, or a restriction on halfspace orientation.

For q=d, any body not resolved by this lemma has every positive-volume fiber of mass strictly below M/2^n. Therefore it has more than 2^n positive-volume fibers. In the intrinsic case the analogous count applies to q-dimensional fibers; fibers of smaller dimension have zero intrinsic mass and do not help this counting argument.

## Projection interior and degeneration

For a full ambient-dimensional convex body C and its projection P onto R^n, every z in int(P) has a full d-dimensional fiber. Indeed choose an interior point (z_0,x_0) of C, so its fiber contains a d-ball. For z in int(P), extend the ray from z_0 through z slightly beyond z to z_1 in P. Then z=(1-t)z_0+t z_1 for some t<1. Choose (z_1,x_1) in C. Convexity places the d-ball (1-t)(x_0+rho B_d)+t x_1 inside C_z. Hence q<d forces int(P) intersect Z^n to be empty. This is a structural observation only; the vertical-thickening proof in candidate 9854c663e6eb01b8 handles all such cases without needing a classification of lattice-free projections.
